findings.where: First screen, Mark's photograph against the slate ground (desktop and phone), and the same key in the Texture specimen's 'Graded for the site' image and the motion sketch's slate card
findings.fault: The photo's purple backdrop has been cut out and replaced with flat slate, so the photo no longer reads as a full-bleed photo of Mark speaking in a room. It reads as a head and shoulders pasted onto a navy panel. The hair has a light fringe against the slate. The shoulder and the podium sign end in hard cut lines. There is no light falloff anywhere. The result looks like a cut-out sticker rather than a real person in real light.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first and asked v7 for a photo of Mark at work, graded but still a photo ('real people in real light', no slick look). A development-bank visitor would object too, because the cut-out halo makes the page look cheap and edited at the moment it should earn trust.

findings.where: Article specimen: the Belt and Road interview photo under the second paragraph
findings.fault: The grade only works on photos with a flat backdrop, so the article photo goes in untreated. Its saturated turquoise sea, orange containers and red banner are far louder than anything else in the slate, grey and blue palette. The Texture note promises that new photos take the same grade, but busy photos, which are most of Mark's, fall outside it. The article page therefore loses the graded look that defines the homepage.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for imagery graded into the house colours (F4) and for a look that survives Angélique's content. A reader moving from the homepage to an article sees two different visual worlds.

findings.where: Article specimen: the blue numbers on the three-item list, and the palette table row that gives blue to 'list numbers'
findings.fault: The page states its own colour rule as 'Grey for reading, blue only where something can be clicked', but the list numbers are blue and can't be clicked. That weakens blue as the signal that something can be clicked, on the very page where links matter.
findings.who_objects: An article reader who has learned that blue means a link, and Angélique, who is told one rule and shown another when she adds lists.
